name: API-Bank: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Tool-Augmented LLMs
venue: EMNLP 2023 (Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, main/long paper, pages 3102-3116; ACL Anthology 2023.emnlp-main.187, DOI 10.18653/v1/2023.emnlp-main.187). Preprint arXiv:2304.08244 (cs.CL), submitted 14 Apr 2023, v2 25 Oct 2023.
authors_affiliation: Minghao Li (Alibaba Group) and Yingxiu Zhao (HKUST) [equal contribution]; Bowen Yu (Alibaba Group, corresponding); Feifan Song (Peking University); Hangyu Li, Haiyang Yu, Fei Huang, Yongbin Li (Alibaba Group); Zhoujun Li (Shenzhen Intelligent Strong Technology Co., Ltd.). Primary affiliation: Alibaba Group (DAMO Academy / Conversational AI).
maintained_repo_url: https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI (official Alibaba DAMO Conversational AI repo hosting the api-bank subdirectory; the benchmark is integrated into downstream harnesses such as CAMEL's apibank.py). No standalone live leaderboard is maintained by the authors.
task_domain: tool-use (tool-augmented LLM benchmark): evaluating an LLM's ability to plan, retrieve, and call external API tools within multi-turn dialogues, with a runnable execution system. Touches decision-making/planning over API call sequences.
problem_setting: Interactive, single-agent, multi-turn tool-use evaluation with a runnable (executable) system. The LLM converses with a user; when it decides a tool is needed it must emit an API-Request in a fixed format [ApiName(key='value', ...)], which the API-Bank system actually executes against initialized databases/external-info stubs and returns an Observation, after which the model generates a natural-language Response. The benchmark grades three escalating ability levels: (1) Call - call the correct API when the relevant API descriptions are given in context (small API pool, slot-filling style); (2) Retrieve+Call - the API pool is hidden/large so the model must first invoke a meta-API 'ToolSearcher'/API Search to retrieve the right API before calling it, with the complex requirement pre-decomposed into single-API simple queries; (3) Plan+Retrieve+Call - the model must autonomously plan and chain multiple Retrieve-then-Call steps within a single turn to satisfy a complex requirement (no pre-decomposition). Evaluation is primarily zero-shot prompting of off-the-shelf LLMs; supervision also exists as a training set (1,888 dialogues from 2,138 APIs over 1,000 domains) used to fine-tune the open model Lynx (initialized from Alpaca-7B / LLaMA-7B). The test set (314 dialogues, 753 API calls, 73 implemented APIs, 8 test domains) is human-annotated and intentionally distribution-shifted from the LLM-synthesized training set to assess generalization.
what_is_retrieved: tools (APIs): API meta-information (name, description, input/output parameters) of candidate tools in a private API Pool/library, retrieved via the special meta-API 'ToolSearcher' (a.k.a. API Search) so the LLM can identify which tool to call.
retrieval_grounding: STATIC external corpus: retrieval targets a fixed API Pool / tool library (the set of implemented APIs and their meta-information). The store is not an agent-written growing/episodic memory; it is a predefined library of tools the user/system has registered.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Fixed top-1 ranking objective per retrieval call: ToolSearcher returns the single API with the highest cosine similarity to the query keywords ('best_matchs', the best match tool). For the Plan+Retrieve+Call ability the agent must, across multiple ToolSearcher calls, recover the complete minimal set of APIs needed to satisfy a multi-step requirement (multi-call completeness emerges from repeated top-1 retrievals), but each individual retrieval is top-1 rather than a variable-size recommendation list.
retrieval_unit: tool-API: one tool's API meta-information record (name + description + input/output parameter specs) is the retrievable unit; ToolSearcher returns the best-matching API record from the library.
index_source: Static corpus built offline: the API Pool/library of registered tools. In the runnable evaluation system 73 APIs are implemented (with initialized databases and hard-coded external-info responses for reproducibility); the training set spans 2,138 APIs over 1,000 domains. The retrievable index is constructed from the meta-information of these predefined APIs; it is not induced online from the agent's own trajectories.
index_structure_topology: Flat vector index over API meta-information: ToolSearcher computes sentence embeddings of all API meta-information in the API Pool and of the query keywords, then ranks by cosine similarity. Each API has a 'desc_for_search' field (name + description concatenation) used as its embedding key. No dependency graph or hierarchical category->API topology is used for retrieval. [uncertain] exact embedding model used by ToolSearcher.
retriever_type: dense (embedding) retriever exposed as a meta-API tool: ToolSearcher obtains sentence embeddings of query keywords and of all API meta-information, computes cosine similarity, and returns the top match. It is an off-the-shelf embedding-similarity retriever invoked by the LLM as a callable API; the LLM acts as the query generator (deciding keywords and when to call ToolSearcher).
retriever_learning_signal: none (off-the-shelf embedding similarity): the ToolSearcher/API Search retriever is a fixed sentence-embedding + cosine-similarity matcher; it is not trained with contrastive, LM-feedback, preference, or RL signals. The only learning in the work is in the GENERATOR side (Lynx is fine-tuned on API-Bank training data, which teaches it to issue ToolSearcher calls and parse retrieved API info), not in the retriever itself.
query_construction: Intent-keyword extraction by the LLM: when an API is needed, the model condenses the user's demand into a few keywords and passes them as the 'keywords' argument to ToolSearcher (e.g. ToolSearcher(keywords='add reminder')). The query is thus an LLM-generated keyword string, not the raw full utterance and not a decomposed sub-query tree.
query_granularity: step/sub-task level: a ToolSearcher query is issued per needed tool. In Retrieve+Call each simple query maps to one retrieval+call; in Plan+Retrieve+Call multiple step-level ToolSearcher queries are issued within a single turn as the plan unfolds. Not a single task-level one-shot retrieval at t=0.
when_to_retrieve: iterative / agent-initiated: the model decides when to call ToolSearcher; an API Search is required before every other (non-search) API call. In Plan+Retrieve+Call, retrieval is interleaved repeatedly across the multi-step rollout (retrieve, call, observe, retrieve again).
retrieval_trigger_signal: Agent-initiated request governed by a fixed protocol rule: the prompt instructs that before using any tool the model must first search for it via ToolSearcher, so retrieval is triggered whenever the model decides it needs a (new) tool to make progress. There is no learned router, token-confidence, or uncertainty signal; the trigger is the agent emitting a ToolSearcher API-Request, constrained by the rule 'an API Search is required before every other API call'.
reranking: None: ToolSearcher returns the single highest-cosine-similarity API ('best_matchs'); there is no second-stage cross-encoder, RRF, or hierarchy-aware reranking.
retrieved_context_refinement: None / minimal: the retrieved API meta-information (name, description, input/output parameters) is returned as an Observation and used directly by the model to format the subsequent API call. No decompose-recompose, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression is applied to the retrieved record.
how_retrieved_used: prompt augmentation within an interactive loop: the retrieved API meta-information (returned as an Observation from ToolSearcher) is read by the model to construct the correct subsequent API-Request (correct name and input parameters), which the system then executes. For Lynx, the same retrieve-then-call pattern is also a fine-tuning training signal (the model learns the ToolSearcher -> API-call pipeline).
planning_integration: retrieve-then-call interleaved inside an agentic ReAct-style loop. Call: no retrieval (APIs given). Retrieve+Call: one retrieve-then-call per pre-decomposed simple query. Plan+Retrieve+Call: the model plans a chain of API calls within a single turn, performing ToolSearcher retrieval before each tool use, executing it, observing the result, and proceeding to the next step until the requirement is met (plan-and-act with per-step retrieval; no MCTS/tree search).
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: per-tool-call within a rollout: each tool the agent needs triggers its own ToolSearcher retrieval, so retrieval is interleaved at the granularity of individual API calls across the multi-step Plan+Retrieve+Call rollout (and once per simple query in Retrieve+Call).
retrieved_item_representation: Structured API meta-information record injected as an Observation: a JSON-like dict with fields {name, description, input_parameters, output_parameters} (the tool's specification). It is raw tool documentation, not a distilled strategy, workflow, program, or latent token.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Raw documentation / single reference item: the retrieved unit is one candidate tool's concrete API specification (name + description + parameter schema), not a distilled strategy, guideline, reusable workflow, or procedural skill.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Primarily fine-tuning to learn the retrieve-then-call pipeline: the paper shows GPT-4's dominant failure mode is 'Failed API Retrieval' (67.86% of GPT-4 errors via in-context use of API Search), whereas the fine-tuned Lynx does not exhibit this failure, indicating fine-tuning teaches robust use of ToolSearcher. No explicit relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor-filtering module is built in; the evaluation system grades whether the correct API was retrieved and called. [uncertain] whether ToolSearcher returns multiple candidates as distractors (example shows it can return more than one record).
memory_type: none: there is no episodic/skill/workflow/graph/latent memory. The API Pool is a static external tool library, not an agent-written memory; dialogue history is passed in-context but not a retrievable learned memory store.
write_back: false: the system does not write new experiences/cases/skills back into a retrievable memory during evaluation. (A separate offline training set is synthesized by the Multi-agent pipeline, but that is dataset construction, not test-time write-back.)
online_growth: false: the API Pool / retrievable tool library is fixed during evaluation; it does not grow from the agent's own outputs at test time.
write_back_trigger: never: no automatic memory write-back exists. API and dialogue data are created offline (human annotation for the test set; LLM Multi-agent synthesis for the training set), not triggered by model success/failure or reflection at inference time.
failure_experience_usage: N/A / none: failed experiences are not stored or retrieved. The paper does perform a manual error-type analysis (e.g., No API Call, API Hallucination, Failed API Retrieval, False API Call Format, Invalid/Missing Input Parameters) to characterize failures, but errors are not persisted as negative cases for retrieval or learning.
memory_evolution_update: N/A: there is no model-written memory to mutate. The static API library is updated only by human/system registration (e.g., hard-coding external-info responses for reproducibility), not via append/dedup/refine of agent memory.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No: tool selection uses a fixed embedding-similarity top-1 retriever (ToolSearcher) invoked by the agent; it is not an RL- or value-learned retrieval policy. The decision of WHEN/WHAT keywords to search is made by the (possibly fine-tuned) LLM via prompting, but the ranking function itself is fixed cosine similarity.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No: single-agent evaluation with a private/user-defined API Pool; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing. (The Multi-agent method uses five collaborating ChatGPT agents, but that is for offline DATA GENERATION, not shared retrievable memory at inference.)
benchmarks: API-Bank (introduced by this paper): runnable evaluation system with 73 implemented APIs, 314 human-annotated tool-use dialogues, 753 API calls, across 8 test domains; split by ability into Call (214 calls), Retrieve+Call (50), Plan+Retrieve+Call (50). Plus an LLM-synthesized training set: 1,888 dialogues, 2,138 APIs, 1,000 domains, 4,149 API calls (broader synthesized corpus reported as 1,008 domains / 2,211 APIs / 2,202 dialogues / 6,135 turns). Also a dataset-quality comparison against ToolAlpaca (Call-only).
benchmark_family: tool (tool/API-use benchmark): API-Bank is a canonical entry in the tool-use benchmark family (alongside ToolBench, APIBench/Gorilla, ToolAlpaca, ToolQA), and is the named tool benchmark in retrieval-augmented tool-use surveys.
baselines: Zero-shot LLMs evaluated on the API-Bank evaluation system: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613), GPT-3.5-turbo (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613), GPT-3 Davinci (text-davinci, 175B), ChatGLM-6B, Alpaca-7B (instruction-tuned LLaMA-7B). The authors' fine-tuned model Lynx-7B (LLaMA-7B initialized from Alpaca, fine-tuned on API-Bank training data) is compared against these. A dataset-quality baseline fine-tunes Alpaca on the ToolAlpaca training set vs Lynx on API-Bank.
key_metrics: (1) Correctness / Accuracy of API calls = #correct predictions / #total predictions, where correctness is judged by whether the predicted API call produces the same database queries/modifications and the same returned results as the annotated call (execution-state consistency in the runnable system). (2) ROUGE-L for the quality of the LLM's post-call natural-language Response. Reported per ability (Call / Retrieve+Call / Plan+Retrieve+Call) and as a Total. No latency/token-cost metrics.
headline_result: On the API-Bank evaluation system (Total, Correctness): GPT-4 60.24%, GPT-3.5-turbo 47.16%, Lynx-7B (fine-tuned) 39.58%, ChatGLM-6B 16.42%, Alpaca-7B 15.19%, GPT-3 Davinci 0.57%. Lynx surpasses Alpaca-7B by 26 points in API Call correctness (49.87% vs 24.06%) and approaches GPT-3.5, while a ~21% Total gap from GPT-4 remains. GPT-4 excels especially at Plan+Retrieve+Call (70.00% vs GPT-3.5's 22.00%).
ablations: (1) Per-ability decomposition (Table 3): correctness drops as required ability escalates (Call > Retrieve+Call > Plan+Retrieve+Call) for most models, exposing planning/retrieval as the bottleneck; GPT-4 is the exception, far stronger on Plan+Retrieve+Call. (2) Instruction-tuning matters: GPT-3 Davinci (175B, not instruction-tuned) scores ~0.5% on Call vs ~20-24% for much smaller instruction-tuned Alpaca-7B/ChatGLM-6B. (3) Fine-tuning effect: Lynx fine-tuned on API-Bank improves Call correctness by 26 pts over base Alpaca-7B and largely eliminates the 'No API Call' and 'False API Call Format' errors, and removes the 'Failed API Retrieval' failure that dominates GPT-4. (4) Error-type analyses (Tables 4-6): Alpaca dominated by 'No API Call' (36.77%); Lynx dominated by 'API Hallucination' (61.38%); GPT-4 dominated by 'Failed API Retrieval' (67.86%). (5) Dataset-quality ablation (Table 7): Lynx fine-tuned on API-Bank data (6,184 samples) beats Alpaca fine-tuned on ToolAlpaca data (10,366 samples) on Call accuracy (54.64 vs 53.88) and Rouge (39.80 vs 39.75) despite fewer samples. (6) Multi-agent vs self-instruct data synthesis: self-instruct yields only 5% usable data (ChatGPT) / 25% (GPT-4), whereas the 5-agent decomposed pipeline produces compliant data at ~98% lower cost ($0.1 vs $8 per dialogue).
evaluation_decoupling: Partial: retrieval quality is assessed indirectly rather than via standalone Recall@k/nDCG. The benchmark grades end-to-end execution-state correctness, and retrieval competence surfaces through (a) the separate Retrieve+Call ability score and (b) the 'Failed API Retrieval' error category in the error analysis. No intrinsic ToolSearcher Recall@k/nDCG numbers are reported separately from task success.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Both outcome and process: outcome is per-API-call execution-state Correctness and final Response ROUGE-L; process is captured via the ability-graded breakdown (planning vs retrieving vs calling) and a six-category error analysis (No API Call, API Hallucination, Failed API Retrieval, False API Call Format, Invalid/Missing Input Parameters, Has Exception) that localizes where in the plan-retrieve-call pipeline models fail.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Reported as data-construction and model-size efficiency rather than retrieval-call counts: Multi-agent synthesis costs ~$0.1/dialogue vs ~$8/dialogue human annotation, a 98% reduction; Lynx-7B approaches GPT-3.5 with far fewer parameters and beats ToolAlpaca-fine-tuned Alpaca with fewer training samples (6,184 vs 10,366). Lynx fine-tuning: LLaMA-7B base, 3 epochs, batch size 256, lr 2e-5. API implementation cost 98 person-days; annotation $8/dialogue; 21.5% of 400 annotated dialogues discarded. No inference latency/token-cost metrics.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Per-retrieval selection is top-1 (ToolSearcher returns the single best-matching API; the example also shows it can return a short candidate list). Total tools surfaced per dialogue grows with the number of ToolSearcher calls the agent issues in Plan+Retrieve+Call. The ability grading is explicitly motivated by input-length limits: when many APIs are defined, all cannot fit in context, so retrieval (top-1 per call) is used instead of injecting the whole pool. No fixed token budget figure is reported.
benchmark_construction_and_size: Evaluation set: 73 runnable APIs implemented in a common framework (98 person-days) with initialized databases and hard-coded external-info responses for reproducibility; 314 human-annotated multi-turn dialogues with 753 API calls over 8 domains, split Call (214) / Retrieve+Call (50) / Plan+Retrieve+Call (50). Annotation: CS-student annotators pair-annotate each dialogue with two extra QA annotators; $8/dialogue; 400 annotated, 21.5% discarded, 314 retained. Training set: synthesized by a novel Multi-agent pipeline of 5 ChatGPT agents (domain -> API (grounded with Public-APIs examples) -> query+ability -> API call & simulated response -> tester agent that discards ~35% non-compliant instances), yielding 1,888 dialogues, 2,138 APIs, 1,000 domains, 4,149 calls (broader run: 1,008 domains / 2,211 APIs / 2,202 dialogues / 6,135 turns); ~$0.1/dialogue (98% cheaper than human). Answer verifiability: high - API-call correctness checked by execution-state consistency in the runnable system; responses scored by ROUGE-L. Difficulty signal: best system GPT-4 reaches only 60.24% Total correctness (vs 80-90% that GPT-3.5 reaches on the concurrent self-instruct-built APIBench/ToolAlpaca), reflecting deliberate real-world difficulty and train/test distribution shift.
builds_on: Self-instruct (Wang et al., 2022) as the data-generation point of departure (extended into the Multi-agent decomposed pipeline because self-instruct under-produces compliant tool-use data); Alpaca-7B / LLaMA-7B (Taori et al., 2023; Touvron et al., 2023) as the base for fine-tuning Lynx; tool-augmented LLM line including Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023), ReAct (Yao et al., 2022), WebGPT (Nakano et al., 2021), and large-scale API integration (TaskMatrix.AI, ChatGPT Plugins).
contrasts_with: Concurrent tool-use benchmarks it positions against in Table 1: APIBench/Gorilla (Patil et al., 2023; single-call, no planning, no multi-turn), ToolAlpaca (Tang et al., 2023; Call-only, self-instruct, narrow domains), ToolBench-1/ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2023b), ToolBench-2 (Xu et al., 2023), ToolQA (Zhuang et al., 2023), and DATESET/Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023). API-Bank claims highest diversity (1,000 domains, 2,138 APIs), highest realism (multi-turn + multi-call), and highest coverage (evaluates Call, Retrieve, and Plan with a runnable execution system and response scoring). It explicitly contrasts its human-annotated, distribution-shifted, harder test set against the self-instruct-generated, narrow-domain test sets where GPT-3.5 already reaches 80-90%.
lineage: Group E (tool-use): a foundational tool-use BENCHMARK with an integral static tool-library retrieval component (the ToolSearcher / API Search meta-API). It sits alongside Gorilla/APIBench and precedes ToolBench/ToolLLM-scale and later tool-retrieval benchmarks (e.g., ToolRet); it is a standard reference benchmark for evaluating retrieve-then-call tool-augmented LLMs and is cited in retrieval-augmented tool-use surveys as the canonical planning+retrieving+calling benchmark.
cbr_cycle_coverage: [Retrieve: yes (ToolSearcher top-1 retrieval of the needed API from the library), Reuse: partial (retrieved API spec is reused to format the call, but it is tool documentation, not a prior solved problem-solution case), Revise: no, Retain: no]. Not a case-based-reasoning system; it retrieves tools, not prior cases.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is a tool-augmented-LLM benchmark with embedding-similarity tool retrieval.
tool_document_engineering: Tool descriptions are engineered into a uniform structured schema {name, description, input_parameters, output_parameters}, and each API additionally has a 'desc_for_search' field (name + description concatenation) that serves as the embedding key for ToolSearcher. No synthetic-query augmentation, expanded summaries, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings are applied to the index; retrieval uses off-the-shelf sentence embeddings over this curated meta-information.
index_content_separation: Partial / progressive disclosure by design: the lightweight API meta-information (name/description/parameter schema) is what is retrieved and injected on demand via ToolSearcher, deliberately because the full API Pool cannot fit in the prompt when many APIs are defined; the heavy runnable API implementation/execution is invoked separately when the model issues the actual API call. So a lightweight searchable index is separated from the executable tool, though the same meta-record is both indexed and shown.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Static, custom function-calling protocol: API-Bank uses its own bespoke API-Request format [ApiName(key='value', ...)] executed by a self-contained runnable system (73 APIs implemented in-house), with ToolSearcher as a built-in retrieval meta-API. The tool index is static/predefined (no live RapidAPI/REST/MCP sync, no automatic CRUD live-sync); external-info APIs are hard-coded to fixed responses to guarantee reproducibility.
tool_dependency_awareness: Implicit, not modeled in retrieval: Plan+Retrieve+Call dialogues require chaining where one API's output feeds another (e.g., GetUserToken -> AddReminder; GetOccupationSalary -> TaxCalculator) and some calls require prerequisite auth tokens, so inter-tool dependencies exist in the tasks. However, ToolSearcher itself does not model dependencies (no dependency graph or dependency-aware reranking); the planning/chaining is left to the LLM agent to infer.
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (not framed as CBR): the closest analogue is that the model reads the retrieved API specification and instantiates a correctly-formatted call from it (parameter slot-filling grounded in the retrieved doc), rather than adapting a prior solved case.
